specAnchors.text: understand why a current in a resistor results in the electrical transfer of energy and an increase in temperature, and how this can be used in a variety of domestic contexts

primer.text: Push a current through a resistor and the resistor warms up — the electrical transfer of energy shows itself as heat. Free electrons jostling through the wire collide and hand over energy, some of which escapes to the surroundings. Far from being a nuisance, that heating effect runs heaters, ovens, hobs, toasters and kettles.

modules.title: The heating effect of a current
modules.opening: Current is a stream of charge, and driving it through a resistor takes work. That work appears as heat: the drifting electrons collide inside the wire, the temperature climbs, and some energy dissipates into the room. Domestic appliances exploit the effect deliberately, turning a glowing element into a hob, a toaster or a kettle.
keyPoints: A current through a resistor or wire transfers energy electrically and warms it.
Free electrons colliding inside the wire raise its temperature.
Some of that energy dissipates into the surroundings by heating.
Domestic appliances put the heating effect to work: heaters, ovens, hobs, toasters and kettles.

low.restatement: Current passing through a resistor makes it hot, because the moving electrons collide inside the wire.
low.analogy: A crowded corridor: people (electrons) bumping into each other and the walls warms everyone up.
low.examPointer: Name the mechanism — collisions of free electrons — whenever a question asks why a resistor heats.

medium.restatement: The same transfer that heats a useful element also dissipates into the surroundings, so every design trades heat delivered against heat lost.
medium.analogy: A kettle versus a phone charger: one sells the heat, the other apologises for it.
medium.examPointer: Domestic-context questions expect named appliances, not just 'gets hot'.

glossary.definition: The rise in temperature produced when a current transfers energy in a resistor.
To spread energy out to the surroundings, often as unwanted heat.
The mobile electrons in a metal that drift and carry the current.

figures.caption: The heating effect of current can be used for many applications such as electric hobs
